clue.text: Entertainer against providing coverage for newspapers, magazines, etc.

indicators.note: to provide coverage for something is to wrap around it, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
the media is the collective term for the press and its kin

explanation.surface: A comic who is opposed to the press giving coverage of his act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coverage' suggests press reporting, but here it means wrapping one word around another.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedian is a performer whose job is to entertain an audience with jokes.

clue.text: Series finale is nothing major

parts.note: the round figure zero looks like the letter
mega is slang for huge or major

explanation.surface: A critic sniffs that the last episode of a show was no big deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'series' is the Greek alphabet, whose final letter is OMEGA.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, hence the end of any sequence.

clue.text: Quit ruffling people's feathers and being threatening!

parts.note: to quit something is to end it
ruffling feathers is an idiom for annoying people

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea to someone to stop provoking everyone and acting menacingly.
explanation.definitionFit: Endangering puts something at risk, which is to threaten its safety.

clue.text: Individuality? It is embodied by Enid Blyton's central characters fantastically

indicators.note: something embodied by a thing is held within its body, so it sits inside
fantastically suggests wild invention, so the letters are rearranged freely

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: central characters are the letters at the middle of the surname

parts.note: the two middle letters of the six-letter surname

explanation.surface: A literary critic claims Blyton's characters express individuality in her fantasy writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Enid Blyton is the British author of the Famous Five children's books; 'characters' here means letters, not people in her stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Identity is the set of qualities that make a person distinct, which is what individuality means.

clue.text: Crazy sergeant maybe drunk some pints

parts.note: a non-com is a non-commissioned officer, of which a sergeant is one example

indicators.note: someone drunk is jumbled and unsteady, so the following words are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sergeant goes mad after downing a few pints.
explanation.definitionFit: Non compos mentis is Latin for not of sound mind, an idiom for mad.

clue.text: No matter how dating starts, it's futile

parts.note: taken as written
goo is sticky, messy matter

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cynic says every romance is doomed however it begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How' only smooths the surface reading and adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no-good is worthless or ineffective, which is close to pointless.

clue.text: Arm lifted up, ultimately revealing huge great lump

indicators.note: in a down entry something lifted up is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: a gun is a firearm, often called an arm

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of each of the words that follow

parts.note: the final letter of each of these three words

explanation.surface: Someone raises an arm and exposes an enormous lump.
explanation.definitionFit: A nugget is a small lump, especially of gold found in the ground.

clue.text: Growth evens out — understood!

indicators.note: putting the even-numbered letters out leaves only the odd ones in place

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A doctor is told that a growth has levelled off, and replies 'Understood!'
explanation.definitionFit: To get something is colloquially to understand it, so 'got it' means understood.

clue.text: Like a dystopian writer, or, um, Fleming perhaps?

parts.note: taken as written
well is a hesitation word, like um
Ian Fleming wrote the James Bond novels

explanation.surface: Musing whether a dystopian writer was like Orwell, or maybe Fleming.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pushes Fleming as an author to compare; only his first name is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwellian describes things in the manner of George Orwell, author of Nineteen Eighty-Four.

clue.text: Tout piano piece on the radio

indicators.note: what is heard on the radio is judged by sound, not spelling

parts.note: a pedal is part of a piano

explanation.surface: A tout plugs a piano composition on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' means a part of the instrument, not a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: To tout goods is to sell them persistently, as a hawker does.

clue.text: Bird near trail next to lake

parts.note: nigh is an old word for near
to trail something behind is to tow it
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's note of a bird close to a lakeside path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is British slang for a person, so a night owl, someone who stays up late, fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A night owl is a person who is active late at night, and bird is informal for a person.

clue.text: Murderer in prison claiming innocence at first

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so the prison word holds the letter

parts.note: the can is slang for jail

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A convicted killer protests innocence from his cell.
explanation.walkthrough: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: Cain is the first killer in the Bible, the archetypal murderer.

clue.text: Young, unsettled lad wrote about occasionally being gutted

indicators.note: about means going round, so the jumbled letters wrap the remaining pair
unsettled means disturbed from its order, so the following words are mixed

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, leaving only the outside letters of the word

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A restless boy who has written now and then, feeling devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' looks like an adverb on 'wrote' but is just the word whose outer letters are kept; 'Young' is a noun, a young animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-year-old is a racehorse or child of that age, a young one.

clue.text: Mathematical method is extremely unusual and therefore complicated

indicators.note: complicated means tangled, so the letters are twisted into a new order
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A maths technique described as very odd and hence hard to follow.
explanation.definitionFit: The rule of three is a method of finding a fourth term in a proportion from three known values.

clue.text: Steer clear of backing favourites on team

indicators.note: one piece placed on another in an across entry is written after it, so the favourites come second

parts.note: a side is a team in sport

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: a teacher's pets are favourites

explanation.surface: Advice to avoid betting on the favourites in the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing favourites' reads like placing bets; backing is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidestep something is to step aside and avoid it.

clue.text: Examples of popular attitudes on given issues

parts.note: something in is fashionable or popular
a stance is a position taken on an issue

explanation.surface: A pollster's report of what the public thinks on certain topics.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case or example of something.

clue.text: Place to hole up in Schiphol Airport

indicators.note: in tells us to look inside the words that follow for a run of letters

parts.note: the last letter of the first word joined to the first three of the second

explanation.surface: Somewhere to hide away at Amsterdam's airport.
explanation.definitionFit: A lair is a hiding place or den, where one holes up.

clue.text: Deposits raised to hide long con?

indicators.note: to hide something is to cover it, so the word goes inside the other
in a down entry a raised word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: to deposit something is to put it down
to itch for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: Bank deposits are pumped up to conceal a lengthy scam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective for the con, but it is the verb, to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: A stitch-up is British slang for a set-up or frame, a kind of con.

clue.text: Limitless anise-flavoured liqueur and sparkling wine

indicators.note: without limits means the word loses its boundaries, its first and last letters

parts.note: pastis is a French aniseed aperitif

explanation.surface: A drinks order of unlimited aniseed spirit plus fizz.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sweet sparkling wine from the Piedmont region of Italy.

clue.text: Key part of match shown in item on TV?

indicators.note: one thing placed on another in an across entry comes after it

parts.note: a television is a set
a point is an item, as on an agenda

explanation.surface: A crucial moment in a game appears in a TV segment.
explanation.walkthrough: Set point is a tennis term for the point that can win a set.
explanation.definitionFit: Set point is the stage in tennis where one player can clinch a set, a decisive moment in a match.

clue.text: After a time, be inclined to put in an appearance

indicators.note: after says which piece is written later, setting the order of the pieces

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time
to tend to do something is to be inclined to

explanation.surface: After a while, someone feels like showing up.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend is to be present at an event, to turn up.

clue.text: Supremely risqué couples wearing nothing

indicators.note: what is worn is held by the wearer, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: naught is an old word for nothing
to couple things is to tie them together

explanation.surface: The raciest pairs are those wearing no clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couples' looks like a noun for pairs of people, but it is a verb meaning joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Naughty can mean mildly indecent, so the superlative is the most risqué.

clue.text: Sharp object that you always stick at the back

indicators.note: at the back points to the final letter of each word

parts.note: the last letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A warning about a pointed thing you keep pushing in behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A tusk is a long pointed tooth, as on an elephant or walrus.

clue.text: Outburst from member of Christian church in Australia

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sudden volley of words or gunfire

definitions.text: member of Christian church in Australia
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Australian slang for a Salvation Army member

explanation.walkthrough: The Salvation Army is a Christian church and charity; Australians call its members Salvos.
explanation.definitionFit: A salvo is a burst of fire or of words, and also Australian slang for a member of the Salvation Army.

clue.text: Small Peugeot? In France, it is most difficult to find

parts.note: S is the clothing abbreviation for small
a Peugeot is a make of car
c'est is French for it is

explanation.surface: In France, a small Peugeot model is the rarest of all.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarcest is the superlative of scarce, meaning in short supply and so hardest to come by.

clue.text: Criticise a Stormzy performance?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to rebuke or knock
second meaning: the music style Stormzy is known for

explanation.walkthrough: Stormzy is a British grime and hip-hop artist.
explanation.definitionFit: To rap is informally to censure, and rap is also the rhythmic spoken music a rapper like Stormzy performs.

clue.text: Pound inspired by British author and poet? I don't think so!

indicators.note: what is inspired is breathed in, so the letter goes inside the name

parts.note: Thomas Hardy wrote novels and poetry
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound

explanation.surface: Was Ezra Pound influenced by a British writer? Doubtful!
explanation.walkthrough: Pound looks like the poet Ezra Pound, but it is the money. L goes inside HARD-Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardly expresses that something is barely or not at all the case, a sceptical denial.

clue.text: Bug consequently found in bygone music device

indicators.note: something found in another is located inside it

parts.note: Apple's iPod music player has been discontinued
so means therefore

explanation.surface: A glitch was therefore found in an old music player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' looks like a software fault, but it is a creature.
explanation.definitionFit: An isopod is a crustacean such as a woodlouse, loosely called a bug.

clue.text: Playing possum protects soldiers and commanders

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it
playing means toying with, so the word is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Feigning death shields both the troops and their leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing possum' is an idiom for pretending to be dead, but here 'Playing' tells you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A supremo is a person in overall charge, a chief or commander.
